# ICP Definition

`sales.market_and_targeting.icp_definition` · v1.0.0 · **draft**

**Which accounts reliably succeed with us, and which reliably do not?**


> Deriving and validating the profile of an account that wins AND retains, stating it in dimensions that can be evaluated before anyone has spoken to the account, and publishing the anti-fit half — disqualifiers, known loss patterns, churn predictors — which is the operationally useful half and the one most often left unwritten. It is NOT market research (which asks whether a market exists), NOT market sizing (which asks how large it is), and NOT qualification (which asks whether one live opportunity is real). Those three are about the market and the deal; this one is about us — which accounts our product, our price and our delivery model actually serve. The output is a classifier, and its worth is measured by what it rejects.

> Deliberately narrow. The temptation on a targeting capability is to load the whole people-and-orgs half of the roster, because "who is in the account" feels like part of who the account is. It is not: committee shape, champion and budget are properties of a live deal, and loading them here lets the compiler produce confident advice about seats nobody has met. Buying Committee, Champion, Decision Maker, Budget and Timeline are all deliberately absent from this manifest and are excluded explicitly in the pre-contact situation. Account is required alongside Company because the two are routinely conflated and only one of them is the unit of fit.

## Outcomes

- A profile stated in dimensions that can be evaluated for an account nobody has spoken to — each dimension checkable from public data or an early conversation, not from a discovery call that has already been paid for.
- A published, enforced disqualifier list. This is the negative outcome and the one that makes the capability operational: a profile that only says yes cannot say no, and saying no is the entire point.
- Every claimed dimension carries its cohort evidence — the won-and-retained, lost and churned accounts that put it there. Dimensions with no evidence behind them stay labelled hypothesis rather than quietly becoming policy.
- Retention evidenced per segment, not only win rate. A segment that closes fast and churns early passes every test a win-rate-only profile can apply.
- Open pipeline scored against the profile, with out-of-profile deals named rather than tolerated.
- A review cadence set, and profile drift raised as a finding for a human rather than absorbed by silently widening the profile.


## Failure modes

- Building the profile from the accounts the company wishes it had. It reads well, describes nobody in the pipeline, and is therefore never used — the most common outcome of this work.
- Listing what customers have in common instead of what separates them from the accounts that were lost. Every won account has a website, a founder and a budget line; only attributes that DIFFER between cohorts carry any information, and a profile built on shared attributes cannot discriminate.
- Firmographics only. Industry and headcount are the cheapest fields to obtain and among the least predictive, so the profile that costs least to build is the one that separates least.
- No disqualifiers, because agreeing on who to reject is politically harder than agreeing on who to want. The anti-fit list is the part that saves time on day one and the part that gets deferred.
- Silent widening. Each out-of-profile deal is waved through as a one-off, no exception is recorded, and within two quarters the profile describes nothing and constrains nobody.
- Written once, then left. A pricing change, a new tier or a shift in the delivery model invalidates half the profile — fit is a joint property of the account and of us — and the document does not move.

## KPIs

| KPI | Unit | Direction | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| in_profile_win_rate_delta | percentage_points | higher_is_better | Win rate inside the profile minus outside. The single test of whether the profile is a classifier. Near zero means everything downstream that depends on it is noise dressed as strategy. |
| in_profile_retention_delta | months | higher_is_better | Retention inside the profile minus outside. The gate the win-rate metric cannot substitute for. |
| out_of_profile_pipeline_share | percent | lower_is_better | How much of open pipeline ignores the profile. Measures whether it is used or merely published. |
| disqualification_rate | percent | target_band | A target band, not a maximum. Near zero means the anti-fit list is not being applied; very high means it has quietly taken over account selection. |
| profile_drift | percent | lower_is_better | Share of recent won-and-retained accounts falling outside the profile. Rising drift is a finding to raise, never a threshold to widen. |
| time_to_fit_verdict | hours | lower_is_better | First touch to a recorded verdict. A profile that needs a research project to apply will not be applied, whatever its quality. |

## Metadata

owner **Sales** · updated 2026-08-08 · review **unreviewed** · confidence **provisional**


> Promoted from stub. Two scoped objects authored — Fit Analysis and Disqualifier — carrying twenty inference patterns between them, of which nine are executable against the pipeline today and eleven are blocked. The executable half is lopsided in a revealing way: every pattern that runs infers fit from DEAL BEHAVIOUR (graph shape, value band, observation mix) and not one infers it from what the account actually is, because no firmographic fact is projected. The single highest-value gap is account.industry / account.employee_count / account.geography as typed Layer 1 facts — the cheapest enrichment in the stack, absent, and it disables the anti-fit half of this capability entirely. The runner-up is a retention signal: the profession validates a profile on retention, Layer 2 emits contract_requested and nothing about the second contract, so the brain can watch every deal close and never learn whether the account was worth closing.
